questions.question: What is the IUPAC name for the structure shown?
questions.answer: The molecule is an amide of methanoic acid ($\text{HCONR}_2$, a C=O bonded to N), and the nitrogen carries two methyl groups, each needing its own locant: $N,N$-dimethylmethanamide.

questions.question: Which of the following compounds is produced in the reaction between hydrochloric acid and calcium carbonate but **not** in the reaction between hydrochloric acid and calcium hydroxide?
questions.answer: $\text{CaCO}_3 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$, whereas $\text{Ca(OH)}_2 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Only the carbonate gives carbon dioxide.

questions.question:
What is the equilibrium expression for the equilibrium system shown?

$$\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4(s) + 4\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 3\text{Fe}(s) + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$$
questions.answer: Pure solids are omitted from the equilibrium expression, and each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient: $K_{eq} = \dfrac{[\text{H}_2\text{O}]^4}{[\text{H}_2]^4}$.

questions.question: Which of the following substances is an Arrhenius base?
questions.answer: An Arrhenius base produces hydroxide ions by dissociation in water. $\text{Sr(OH)}_2 \rightarrow \text{Sr}^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^-$ contains $\text{OH}^-$ ions; the others are bases only in the Brønsted–Lowry sense (they accept protons).

questions.question: Which compound listed below will react in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid with the product of its own oxidation to produce an ester?
questions.answer: Propan-1-ol is a primary alcohol, so it oxidises (via propanal) to propanoic acid. The alcohol and the acid then esterify (conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ catalyst) to give propyl propanoate. Propan-2-ol oxidises to a ketone, which cannot form an ester; propanal and propanoic acid are not alcohols.

questions.question: Which compound will produce a peak at 210 ppm in $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR spectroscopy?
questions.answer: Carbonyl carbons of aldehydes and ketones appear at about 190–220 ppm. Pentanal's CHO carbon gives the peak near 210 ppm (a carboxylic acid C=O is lower, about 160–185 ppm; C–O and C–N carbons are about 25–70 ppm).

questions.question:
Consider the equilibrium system shown for the production of nitrosyl chloride (NOCl).

$$2\text{NO}(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NOCl}(g) \qquad \Delta H = -75.5\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Which of the following conditions will maximise the equilibrium yield of nitrosyl chloride?
questions.answer: The forward reaction reduces the number of gas moles (3 → 2), so high pressure shifts equilibrium right (Le Chatelier). The forward reaction is exothermic, so low temperature also shifts equilibrium right.

questions.question:
The titration curve below shows the pH as titrant is added (equivalence point at about 25 mL; the pH starts near 3, rises slowly through a buffer region to about 6, jumps to about 11, then levels off near 12.5).

Which of the following titrations would result in this titration curve?
options: 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$ with 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH
0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ HCl with 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH
0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ HCl with 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{NH}_3$
questions.answer: The starting pH (~3) and the gradual buffer region before equivalence show a weak acid (propanoic acid); the high final pH (~12.5) and the equivalence point above 7 show a strong base (NaOH). A strong acid would start near pH 1, and ammonia would not take the pH above about 11.

questions.question:
The titration curve below shows the pH as titrant is added (equivalence point at about 25 mL; the pH starts near 3, rises slowly through a buffer region to about 6, jumps to about 11, then levels off near 12.5).

Which of the following indicators is most suitable for determining the endpoint of this titration?
questions.answer: The vertical section of the curve (equivalence point of a weak acid–strong base titration) is at about pH 7–11, centred around pH 8–9. Phenolphthalein changes colour within this range.

questions.question: An aqueous solution containing which substance is most likely to have a pH of 9?
questions.answer: Amines are weak bases: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_3^+ + \text{OH}^-$, giving a basic solution. Methanol and butanal are neutral; propanoic acid is acidic.

questions.question: In proton NMR, what do the relative peak areas indicate about a pure substance?
options: The number of protons in the molecule.
The ratio of protons in different environments.
The proximity of the proton to an electronegative element.
The molecular weight of the molecule.
questions.answer: Peak area (integration) is proportional to the number of hydrogens in each environment, so the relative areas give the ratio of protons in the different environments (not the absolute number). Proximity to electronegative atoms affects chemical shift instead.

questions.question: Infrared spectroscopy of a pure compound produces a broad peak centred at 3415 cm$^{-1}$. Which series of organic compounds is the unknown compound likely to belong to?
questions.answer: A broad absorption at about 3230–3550 cm$^{-1}$ is the hydrogen-bonded O–H stretch of an alcohol. A carboxylic acid O–H is much broader and lower (about 2500–3000 cm$^{-1}$).

questions.question: Which of the following mixtures of aqueous species will form a buffer solution when both species have a concentration of approximately 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$?
questions.answer: A buffer is a weak acid and its conjugate base in similar amounts. Methanoic acid is a weak acid and methanoate is its conjugate base. HCl is a strong acid, so Cl⁻ is not an effective base.

questions.question:
The graph shows changes in the reaction quotient $Q$ over time for the equilibrium system

$$\text{X}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{Y}(g) \qquad \Delta H > 0$$

At $t_1$, $Q$ (already at equilibrium) begins to rise gradually from its equilibrium value to a new, higher constant value. At $t_2$, $Q$ drops suddenly, then rises gradually back to the same value it had just before $t_2$.

Which of the following could be the changes made at $t_1$ and $t_2$?
options: $t_1$: decrease in temperature; $t_2$: addition of X
$t_1$: decrease in temperature; $t_2$: removal of X
$t_1$: increase in temperature; $t_2$: addition of Y
$t_1$: increase in temperature; $t_2$: removal of Y
questions.answer: $Q = \dfrac{[\text{Y}]}{[\text{X}]}$. At $t_1$ there is no sudden change, but $Q$ settles at a higher value, so $K_{eq}$ increased: for an endothermic reaction this means the temperature was increased. At $t_2$, $Q$ suddenly falls and returns to the same value (same $K_{eq}$, so same temperature): a concentration change that lowers $[\text{Y}]/[\text{X}]$, i.e. removal of Y (or addition of X — but addition of X is not paired with a temperature increase in the options).

questions.question: Which set of peaks would be likely found in the mass spectrum of 2,2-dimethylpropanal?
questions.answer: 2,2-Dimethylpropanal is $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-CHO}$, $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$, $M = 86$ (molecular ion at 86). Likely fragments: $\text{CH}_3^+$ (15), $\text{CHO}^+$ (29), $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$ (57) and $[M-\text{CH}_3]^+$ (71).

questions.question: Which infrared spectrum was most likely produced from a pure sample of propanone?
questions.answer: Propanone has a C=O but no O–H. Spectrum C shows a very strong C=O absorption near 1715 cm$^{-1}$ and C–H near 3000 cm$^{-1}$ with no O–H band. A has a sharp O–H (free) band near 3600 cm$^{-1}$, B a broad O–H band (alcohol), and D has no strong C=O peak.

questions.question:
In an experiment to determine the $K_{sp}$ value of barium fluoride, 1.0 mL samples containing barium ions were each added to a 1.0 mL solution containing fluoride ions. The results are given below.

| Sample | Initial [Ba$^{2+}$] (mol L$^{-1}$), volume 1.0 mL | Initial [F$^-$] (mol L$^{-1}$), volume 1.0 mL | Observation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.010 | 0.026 | No precipitate |
| 2 | 0.010 | 0.028 | No precipitate |
| 3 | 0.010 | 0.030 | Faint white precipitate |
| 4 | 0.010 | 0.032 | White precipitate |

Which of the following could be the $K_{sp}$ value of barium fluoride?
questions.answer: Mixing halves each concentration: $[\text{Ba}^{2+}] = 0.0050$. Sample 2: $[\text{F}^-] = 0.014$, $Q = 0.0050 \times 0.014^2 = 9.8 \times 10^{-7}$ (no precipitate, so $K_{sp} > 9.8 \times 10^{-7}$). Sample 3: $[\text{F}^-] = 0.015$, $Q = 0.0050 \times 0.015^2 = 1.1 \times 10^{-6}$ (precipitate, so $K_{sp} \le 1.1 \times 10^{-6}$). Only $1.0 \times 10^{-6}$ lies in this range.

questions.question: When ethene is reacted completely with hydrogen bromide, 7.27 L of the product is obtained at 25.0 °C and 120 kPa. What is the mass of ethene that was reacted?
questions.answer: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{HBr} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}$ (1 : 1). Treating the product as a gas: $n = \dfrac{PV}{RT} = \dfrac{120 \times 7.27}{8.314 \times 298.15} = 0.352$ mol. $m(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4) = 0.352 \times 28.05 = 9.87$ g.

questions.question: A salt has a $K_{sp}$ value of $4.3 \times 10^{-10}$ and a molar solubility of $2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$. Which of the following represents the formula of this salt?

1.242 kg of a single polymer with the repeating unit shown below (–O–CH₂CH₂–O–CO–C₆H₄–CO–, i.e. a polyester of ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid) was obtained after a polymerisation reaction.

What mass of water is released during this polymerisation reaction?
questions.answer: Repeating unit $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_8\text{O}_4$, $M = 192.2$ g mol$^{-1}$. $n(\text{units}) = \dfrac{1242}{192.2} = 6.46$ mol. Each repeating unit contains two ester links, so 2 water molecules are released per unit: $n(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = 12.9$ mol, $m = 12.9 \times 18.02 = 233$ g.

questions.question: Using balanced chemical equations, show that the $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ ion can react with both strong acids and strong bases.
questions.answer:
With a strong acid ($\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ acts as a base, accepting a proton):
$$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-(aq) + \text{H}^+(aq) \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4(aq)$$
With a strong base ($\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ acts as an acid, donating a proton):
$$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{HPO}_4^{2-}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
So $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ is amphiprotic. ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ or a named strong acid such as HCl, and any metal hydroxide, are equally acceptable.)

questions.question: Calculate the pH of 0.20 mol L$^{-1}$ hydrazoic acid ($\text{HN}_3$, $K_a = 1.9 \times 10^{-5}$).
questions.answer:
$\text{HN}_3(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+(aq) + \text{N}_3^-(aq)$

| | $\text{HN}_3$ | $\text{H}^+$ | $\text{N}_3^-$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | 0.20 | 0 | 0 |
| C | $-x$ | $+x$ | $+x$ |
| E | $0.20 - x$ | $x$ | $x$ |

$K_a = \dfrac{[\text{H}^+][\text{N}_3^-]}{[\text{HN}_3]} = \dfrac{x^2}{0.20 - x} \approx \dfrac{x^2}{0.20} = 1.9 \times 10^{-5}$ (assuming $x \ll 0.20$)

$x^2 = 3.8 \times 10^{-6}$, so $x = [\text{H}^+] = 1.9 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$

$\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(1.9 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.71$ (the same result is obtained without the approximation).

questions.question:
Hydrogen iodide decomposes when heated to hydrogen and iodine:

$$2\text{HI}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2(g) + \text{I}_2(g)$$

Give the equilibrium expression for this reaction.
questions.answer: $$K_{eq} = \frac{[\text{H}_2][\text{I}_2]}{[\text{HI}]^2}$$

questions.question:
Hydrogen iodide decomposes when heated to hydrogen and iodine:

$$2\text{HI}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2(g) + \text{I}_2(g)$$

In an experiment, 1.75 mol of hydrogen iodide was placed in a 1.00 L vessel at a constant temperature. At equilibrium, the concentration of iodine gas was 0.168 mol L$^{-1}$.

What is the $K_{eq}$ value at this temperature?

Hydrogen iodide decomposes when heated to hydrogen and iodine:

$$2\text{HI}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2(g) + \text{I}_2(g)$$

Explain what would happen to the value of $K_{eq}$ if a catalyst was added at constant temperature.
questions.answer: $K_{eq}$ stays the same. A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, increasing the rates of the forward and reverse reactions by the same factor. The forward and reverse rates therefore stay equal, the equilibrium concentrations of $\text{H}_2$, $\text{I}_2$ and HI are unchanged (equilibrium is simply reached faster), so $K_{eq}$ is unchanged.

questions.question:
100.0 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide is mixed with 100.0 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ nitric acid in a cardboard cup. The initial temperature of each solution is 24.30 °C and the resulting solution has a temperature of 31.15 °C.

You can assume that there is no volume change upon reaction, and that the resulting solution has a density of 1.04 g mL$^{-1}$ and a specific heat capacity of 4.03 J K$^{-1}$ g$^{-1}$.

Calculate the enthalpy of neutralisation for this reaction.
questions.answer:
$m(\text{solution}) = 200.0\ \text{mL} \times 1.04\ \text{g mL}^{-1} = 208\ \text{g}$

$\Delta T = 31.15 - 24.30 = 6.85\ \text{K}$

$q = mc\Delta T = 208 \times 4.03 \times 6.85 = 5740\ \text{J} = 5.74\ \text{kJ}$

$n(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = n(\text{HNO}_3) = n(\text{NaOH}) = 1.00 \times 0.1000 = 0.100\ \text{mol}$

$\Delta H = -\dfrac{5.74\ \text{kJ}}{0.100\ \text{mol}} = -57.4\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ (negative because the reaction is exothermic).

questions.question:
The synthesis of ammonia from its elements is an equilibrium process:

$$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)$$

The table shows the value of $K_{eq}$ for this reaction at a range of temperatures.

| Temperature (K) | 390 | 400 | 420 | 430 | 440 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $K_{eq}$ | 90 | 44 | 12 | 6.4 | 3.6 |

Plot this data on a graph of $K_{eq}$ against temperature, including a curved line of best fit.
questions.answer:
Plot temperature (K) on the horizontal axis (e.g. 380–450 K) and $K_{eq}$ on the vertical axis (e.g. 0–100), with labelled axes and an even scale that uses most of the grid. Plot the five points (390, 90), (400, 44), (420, 12), (430, 6.4), (440, 3.6) accurately and draw a smooth curve through them: $K_{eq}$ falls steeply at first, then levels off, approaching zero at higher temperatures (a decaying curve, concave up).

Marking: correct labelled axes, appropriate scale (graph uses at least 25% of each axis), accurate plotting, smooth curve through all points.

questions.question:
The synthesis of ammonia from its elements is an equilibrium process:

$$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)$$

The table shows the value of $K_{eq}$ for this reaction at a range of temperatures.

| Temperature (K) | 390 | 400 | 420 | 430 | 440 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $K_{eq}$ | 90 | 44 | 12 | 6.4 | 3.6 |

Using a graph of this data with a curved line of best fit, estimate $K_{eq}$ at 410 K.
questions.answer: Reading from the curve at 410 K (between 44 at 400 K and 12 at 420 K, the curve sagging below the straight line joining them): $K_{eq} \approx 23$ (values of about 22–27 read from a reasonable curve are accepted).

questions.question:
The synthesis of ammonia from its elements is an equilibrium process:

$$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)$$

The table shows the value of $K_{eq}$ for this reaction at a range of temperatures.

| Temperature (K) | 390 | 400 | 420 | 430 | 440 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $K_{eq}$ | 90 | 44 | 12 | 6.4 | 3.6 |

At 410 K, $K_{eq}$ is approximately 23. A system at 410 K is found to have $[\text{N}_2] = 0.24$ mol L$^{-1}$, $[\text{H}_2] = 1.1$ mol L$^{-1}$ and $[\text{NH}_3] = 1.6$ mol L$^{-1}$.

Show that this system is not at equilibrium and use $Q$ and $K_{eq}$ to explain how the system will shift to reach equilibrium.
questions.answer:
$$Q = \frac{[\text{NH}_3]^2}{[\text{N}_2][\text{H}_2]^3} = \frac{(1.6)^2}{(0.24)(1.1)^3} = \frac{2.56}{0.319} = 8.0$$

$Q \neq K_{eq}$ ($Q \approx 8 < K_{eq} \approx 23$), so the system is not at equilibrium.

For $Q$ to increase to $K_{eq}$, the forward reaction is favoured: $[\text{NH}_3]$ increases while $[\text{N}_2]$ and $[\text{H}_2]$ decrease, until $Q = K_{eq}$.

questions.question:
The synthesis of ammonia from its elements is an equilibrium process:

$$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)$$

The table shows the value of $K_{eq}$ for this reaction at a range of temperatures.

| Temperature (K) | 390 | 400 | 420 | 430 | 440 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $K_{eq}$ | 90 | 44 | 12 | 6.4 | 3.6 |

Is the production of ammonia exothermic or endothermic? Justify your answer using Le Châtelier's principle and the data provided.
questions.answer:
The forward reaction (production of ammonia) is exothermic.

The data show that as temperature increases, $K_{eq}$ decreases (from 90 at 390 K to 3.6 at 440 K). A smaller $K_{eq}$ means the equilibrium mixture contains relatively less $\text{NH}_3$ and more $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$, i.e. the reverse reaction is favoured at higher temperature.

By Le Châtelier's principle, increasing the temperature favours the endothermic direction (which absorbs the added heat). Since the reverse reaction is favoured, the reverse reaction is endothermic and so the forward reaction, producing ammonia, is exothermic.

questions.question:
Soap can be used as a cleaning agent due to its ability to stabilise emulsions.

Draw a labelled diagram to show the structure of a soap molecule.
questions.answer: A soap is the salt of a long-chain fatty acid, e.g. sodium stearate $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_{16}\text{COO}^-\ \text{Na}^+$. The diagram shows a long hydrocarbon tail labelled **non-polar / hydrophobic end**, attached to a negatively charged carboxylate head ($-\text{COO}^-$) labelled **ionic / polar / hydrophilic end**.

questions.question:
Soap can be used as a cleaning agent due to its ability to stabilise emulsions.

Explain how soap can act as a cleaning agent.
questions.answer:
Grease and oil are non-polar and do not dissolve in water. When soap is added, the non-polar hydrocarbon tails of the soap anions dissolve in the grease, attracted by dispersion forces, while the ionic carboxylate heads remain in the water, attracted to water molecules by ion–dipole forces (and hydrogen bonding).

The soap anions surround small droplets of grease to form **micelles**: the grease is in the centre, and the outside of each micelle is covered in negatively charged heads. Because the micelles all carry a negative surface charge they repel each other and do not coalesce, so the grease is held as a stable emulsion of droplets suspended in the water. The emulsified grease is then washed away with the rinse water, cleaning the surface.

questions.question:
Two esters, A and B, have molecular formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2$. Ester A is ethyl propanoate ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, first structure) and ester B is *tert*-butyl methanoate ($\text{HCOOC(CH}_3)_3$, second structure). Their proton NMR data are:

**Ester A**

| Chemical shift (ppm) | Relative peak area | Splitting |
|---|---|---|
| 1.05 | 3 | triplet |
| 1.16 | 3 | triplet |
| 2.26 | 2 | quartet |
| 4.11 | 2 | quartet |

**Ester B**

| Chemical shift (ppm) | Relative peak area | Splitting |
|---|---|---|
| 1.42 | 9 | singlet |
| 9.60 | 1 | singlet |

State **two** differences between the proton NMR data and relate these to the structure of the two esters.
questions.answer:
**Difference 1 – number of peaks.** Ester A gives 4 peaks but ester B gives only 2. A has four different hydrogen environments (two different $\text{CH}_3$ groups and two different $\text{CH}_2$ groups, one next to C=O and one next to O), whereas in B the three methyl groups of the *tert*-butyl group are equivalent (one environment, 9H) and the other environment is the single H on the HCO group.

**Difference 2 – splitting pattern.** Ester A gives two triplets and two quartets, while ester B gives two singlets. In A each $\text{CH}_3$ is next to a $\text{CH}_2$ (2 neighbouring H → triplet) and each $\text{CH}_2$ is next to a $\text{CH}_3$ (3 neighbouring H → quartet), i.e. A contains two ethyl ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$–) groups. In B the methyl groups are attached to a quaternary carbon with no hydrogens, and the HCO hydrogen is attached to a carbon with no H neighbours, so both sets of protons are isolated and appear as singlets.

(Other valid differences: B has a peak at 9.60 ppm from the H on the carbonyl carbon (H–C=O), which A lacks; the peak-area ratios are 3:3:2:2 for A but 9:1 for B.)

questions.question:
The pH of two 100 mL solutions, X and Y, was measured before and after 1.00 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide solution was added to each.

| | Initial pH | Final pH |
|---|---|---|
| Solution X | 1.22 | 1.31 |
| Solution Y | 4.76 | 4.84 |

One of these solutions contains a weak acid and its conjugate base, both at a concentration of 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$; the other contains a 0.060 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of hydrochloric acid.

By performing a relevant calculation, show that Solution X is the 0.060 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of hydrochloric acid.
questions.answer:
HCl is a strong acid and fully ionises, so $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 0.0600$ mol L$^{-1}$:
$$\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(0.0600) = 1.22$$
This equals the initial pH of solution X, so X is the 0.060 mol L$^{-1}$ HCl.

(Alternatively: $n(\text{HCl}) = 0.006$ mol, $n(\text{NaOH}) = 0.001$ mol, excess HCl $= 0.005$ mol in 0.101 L, $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 0.0495$ mol L$^{-1}$, pH $= 1.31$ = final pH of X.)

questions.question:
The pH of two 100 mL solutions, X and Y, was measured before and after 1.00 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide solution was added to each.

| | Initial pH | Final pH |
|---|---|---|
| Solution X | 1.22 | 1.31 |
| Solution Y | 4.76 | 4.84 |

One of these solutions contains a weak acid and its conjugate base, both at a concentration of 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$; the other contains a 0.060 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of hydrochloric acid.

Calculate the $K_a$ of the weak acid.
questions.answer:
Solution Y is the buffer with $[\text{HA}] = [\text{A}^-]$. Since $K_a = \dfrac{[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+][\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]}$, when $[\text{HA}] = [\text{A}^-]$, $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = K_a$, so $\text{p}K_a = \text{pH} = 4.76$.
$$K_a = 10^{-4.76} = 1.7 \times 10^{-5}$$

questions.question:
The pH of two 100 mL solutions, X and Y, was measured before and after 1.00 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide solution was added to each.

| | Initial pH | Final pH |
|---|---|---|
| Solution X | 1.22 | 1.31 |
| Solution Y | 4.76 | 4.84 |

One of these solutions contains a weak acid and its conjugate base, both at a concentration of 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$; the other contains a 0.060 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of hydrochloric acid.

When 1.00 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide solution is added to 100 mL of water, the pH increases from 7.00 to 12.00.

Explain why adding 1.00 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide solution to both solution X and solution Y does not change the pH of either appreciably.
questions.answer:
Both solutions receive $n(\text{OH}^-) = 1.00 \times 0.00100 = 1.00$ mmol.

**Solution X:** contains $100\ \text{mL} \times 0.0600 = 6.00$ mmol HCl. After neutralising 1.00 mmol, 5.00 mmol of HCl remains, so the strong acid is still present in large excess; $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ falls only slightly (0.0600 → 0.0495 mol L$^{-1}$) and the pH rises only from 1.22 to 1.31.

**Solution Y:** is a buffer containing 10.0 mmol of the weak acid HA and 10.0 mmol of its conjugate base A$^-$. The added hydroxide reacts with the weak acid: $\text{HA} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{A}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$, leaving 9.00 mmol HA and 11.00 mmol A$^-$. The added OH$^-$ is consumed rather than remaining free in solution, and the ratio $[\text{A}^-]/[\text{HA}]$ stays close to 1, so the pH stays close to the p$K_a$ (4.76 → 4.84).

questions.question:
Linalool (3,7-dimethylocta-1,6-dien-3-ol) is a compound found in many flowers and spices. Its structural formula is shown: $\text{CH}_2\text{=CH-C(OH)(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-CH=C(CH}_3)_2$.

State the names of the **two** functional groups in linalool.
questions.answer:
1. Alkene (carbon–carbon double bond)
2. Alcohol (hydroxyl group) — specifically a tertiary alcohol.

questions.question:
Linalool (3,7-dimethylocta-1,6-dien-3-ol) is a compound found in many flowers and spices. Its structural formula is shown: $\text{CH}_2\text{=CH-C(OH)(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-CH=C(CH}_3)_2$.

Draw the structural formula of the organic product formed when linalool reacts with each of the following reagents under the stated conditions:

1. $\text{H}_2(g)$, Pd catalyst
2. $\text{Br}_2(aq)$
3. $\text{HCOOH}(aq)$, $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ catalyst, heated under reflux
questions.answer:
1. **$\text{H}_2$/Pd:** both C=C double bonds are hydrogenated, the OH is unchanged: 3,7-dimethyloctan-3-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{-C(OH)(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3)_2$.
2. **$\text{Br}_2$:** bromine adds across both double bonds: 1,2,6,7-tetrabromo-3,7-dimethyloctan-3-ol, $\text{CH}_2\text{Br-CHBr-C(OH)(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-CHBr-CBr(CH}_3)_2$.
3. **HCOOH / $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ / reflux:** esterification of the OH group with methanoic acid (both C=C remain): linalyl methanoate (3,7-dimethylocta-1,6-dien-3-yl methanoate), $\text{H-CO-O-C(CH}_3\text{)(CH=CH}_2\text{)-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-CH=C(CH}_3)_2$.

questions.question:
The compound responsible for the hot taste of chillies, capsaicin, is shown. It has a long hydrocarbon chain attached through an amide group to a benzene ring bearing –OH and –OCH₃ groups. Drinking full cream milk, which contains fat, is recommended after eating meals containing lots of chilli as it reduces the hot taste on the tongue.

Explain why milk is better than water in removing capsaicin from the tongue.
questions.answer:
Although capsaicin has some polar groups (–OH, –O–, amide), most of the molecule is a large non-polar hydrocarbon chain and benzene ring, so overall it is largely non-polar. It cannot form enough hydrogen bonds / dipole–dipole attractions with water to overcome the strong hydrogen bonding between water molecules, so it is only very slightly soluble in water and water does not remove it from the tongue.

Full cream milk contains fat, which is non-polar. The non-polar parts of capsaicin form dispersion forces with the fat molecules, comparable in strength to those between capsaicin molecules, so capsaicin dissolves readily in the fat (milk is also an emulsion of fat droplets stabilised by emulsifiers, which can take up capsaicin). Capsaicin is therefore far more soluble in milk than in water, and milk carries it away from the tongue.

questions.question:
Three bottles, known to contain pentan-1-ol, pentan-3-ol and 2-methylbutan-2-ol, are missing labels.

Suggest how a student could distinguish between the three alcohols using one or more chemical tests.
questions.answer:
Warm a sample of each alcohol with acidified potassium dichromate solution.
- 2-methylbutan-2-ol (tertiary) is not oxidised: the solution stays orange.
- Pentan-1-ol (primary) and pentan-3-ol (secondary) are oxidised: the solution turns from orange to green.

To distinguish these two, heat each under reflux with excess acidified dichromate, then test the product with sodium carbonate solution. Pentan-1-ol is oxidised to pentanoic acid, which gives effervescence ($\text{CO}_2$ bubbles); pentan-3-ol is oxidised to pentan-3-one, a ketone, which gives no effervescence.

(Alternative accepted: Lucas reagent — the tertiary alcohol turns cloudy immediately, the secondary turns cloudy after some minutes, and the primary remains a clear, colourless solution.)

questions.question:
Three bottles, known to contain pentan-1-ol, pentan-3-ol and 2-methylbutan-2-ol, are missing labels.

The student can use a combination of infrared spectroscopy, mass spectrometry and $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR to confirm the contents of the three bottles. Evaluate the suitability of these techniques for this purpose.
questions.answer:
**Infrared spectroscopy — not suitable on its own.** All three compounds are alcohols with an O–H group, so all would show a broad O–H absorption at about 3230–3550 cm$^{-1}$ and C–H and C–O absorptions. The spectra would differ only subtly in the fingerprint region, so IR confirms that each bottle contains an alcohol but cannot reliably identify which isomer is which.

**Mass spectrometry — limited suitability.** The three alcohols are isomers ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$) with the same molar mass, so all give a molecular ion peak at $m/z = 88$. Fragmentation patterns differ somewhat, but the molecular ion alone cannot distinguish them.

**$^{13}\text{C}$ NMR — highly suitable.** Each alcohol has a different number of carbon environments because of its symmetry:
- pentan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$: 5 environments → 5 peaks;
- pentan-3-ol, $(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2)_2\text{CHOH}$: symmetrical → 3 peaks;
- 2-methylbutan-2-ol, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$: 4 environments → 4 peaks.

**Judgement:** $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR alone can identify each bottle; IR and MS are useful only to confirm the alcohol functional group and the molar mass, so the combination is suitable mainly because of the $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR data.

questions.question:
Alkene A reacts with gaseous hydrogen chloride to form two isomers, B and C, with molecular formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Cl}$. A sequence of reactions for each compound is shown below:

- B → (substitution reaction using dilute NaOH(aq)) → D → (oxidation using acidified potassium dichromate solution) → **no reaction**
- C → (substitution reaction using dilute NaOH(aq)) → E → (oxidation using acidified potassium dichromate solution) → F

Determine the structural formulae of the compounds A to F.
questions.answer:
D is not oxidised, so it is a tertiary alcohol; the only tertiary $\text{C}_4$ alcohol is 2-methylpropan-2-ol, so the alkene must be branched.

- **A:** 2-methylpropene (methylpropene), $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3)_2$
- **B:** 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCl}$
- **C:** 1-chloro-2-methylpropane, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{Cl}$
- **D:** 2-methylpropan-2-ol, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH}$ (tertiary, not oxidised)
- **E:** 2-methylpropan-1-ol, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{OH}$ (primary)
- **F:** 2-methylpropanoic acid, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCOOH}$ (2-methylpropanal, from partial oxidation, was also accepted)

(But-1-ene would give 2-chlorobutane and 1-chlorobutane, whose alcohols are secondary and primary — both oxidisable — so it does not fit.)

questions.question:
Periclase is a mineral composed of magnesium oxide ($M = 40.31$ g mol$^{-1}$). A 0.4802 g ore sample containing periclase is treated with 50.00 mL of 0.5020 mol L$^{-1}$ hydrochloric acid. The acid reacts with the magnesium oxide, but not with the other components of the ore sample. After reaction and filtration, the solution is made up to 250.0 mL in a volumetric flask. 25.00 mL aliquots of this solution are titrated with 0.1034 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide, requiring an average of 12.90 mL to reach the endpoint.

Calculate the percentage by mass of magnesium oxide in the periclase ore sample.
questions.answer:
$\text{MgO}(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$; $\ \text{HCl} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

$n(\text{HCl added}) = 0.05000 \times 0.5020 = 25.10$ mmol

$n(\text{NaOH}) = 0.01290 \times 0.1034 = 1.334$ mmol $= n(\text{HCl excess in aliquot})$

$n(\text{HCl excess, total}) = 1.334 \times \dfrac{250.0}{25.00} = 13.34$ mmol

$n(\text{HCl reacted with MgO}) = 25.10 - 13.34 = 11.76$ mmol

$n(\text{MgO}) = \dfrac{11.76}{2} = 5.881$ mmol

$m(\text{MgO}) = 5.881 \times 10^{-3} \times 40.31 = 0.2371$ g

$\%\text{MgO} = \dfrac{0.2371}{0.4802} \times 100 = 49.37\%$

questions.question:
Red iron(III) thiocyanate is produced in the following equilibrium reaction:

$$\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq) + \text{SCN}^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons [\text{FeSCN}]^{2+}(aq)$$

At equilibrium at 298 K there are 0.00540 mol of $\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq)$, 0.00823 mol of $\text{SCN}^-(aq)$ and 0.0631 mol of $[\text{FeSCN}]^{2+}(aq)$ in a 100.0 mL solution.

What mass of pure sodium hydroxide should be added to increase the amount of $\text{SCN}^-(aq)$ to 0.00944 mol at equilibrium?

Compound Q is an organic compound which contains roughly 19% nitrogen by mass. The infrared, $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR and $^1\text{H}$ NMR spectra of compound Q are shown (in that order).

- IR: a weak, fairly sharp absorption near 3400 cm$^{-1}$; strong C–H absorptions just below 3000 cm$^{-1}$; no absorption near 1700 cm$^{-1}$.
- $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR: three peaks, at about 23, 35 and 50 ppm.
- $^1\text{H}$ NMR (relative areas): 3.25 ppm (1H, singlet), 2.9 ppm (1H, multiplet), 2.55 ppm (3H, singlet), 1.15 ppm (6H, doublet).

$^1\text{H}$ NMR chemical shift data:

| Type of proton | δ/ppm |
|---|---|
| R–CH$_3$ | 0.9–1.0 |
| R–CH$_2$–R | 1.2–1.5 |
| R–CHR$_2$ | 1.5–2.0 |
| R–C≡C–H | 2.0–3.1 |
| –CO–CH$_2$– (aldehydes, ketones, esters) | 2.1–2.7 |
| R–CH$_2$–NH$_2$ or CHR–NH$_2$ | 2.4–3.0 |
| R–CH$_2$–NHR or CHR–NHR | 2.5–3.1 |
| –CH$_2$–O– (alcohols, ethers, esters) | 3.3–4.8 |
| R–OH | 1–6 |
| R–NH$_2$ | 1–5 |
| R–NHR | 1–5 |
| R$_2$C=CHR (alkene) | 4.5–7.0 |
| R–CONH–R (amide) | 5–9 |
| R–CHO | 9.4–10.0 |
| R–COOH | 9.0–13.0 |

Draw and name compound Q and justify your choice using all the information provided.
questions.answer:
**Compound Q: $N$-methylpropan-2-amine**, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH-NH-CH}_3$.

**% composition:** if Q contains one N atom, $M \approx \dfrac{14.01}{0.19} \approx 74$ g mol$^{-1}$. The $^1$H NMR integrations total 11 H. Removing N and 11 H (25) from 74 leaves 49, about 4 C. Formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{11}\text{N}$ ($M = 73.14$; %N $= 19.2\%$ ✓), a saturated amine.

**IR:** the absorption near 3400 cm$^{-1}$ is an N–H stretch; a single weak peak suggests a secondary amine. There is no C=O (no peak near 1700 cm$^{-1}$), so it is not an amide.

**$^{13}$C NMR:** only 3 peaks for 4 carbons, so two carbons are equivalent (symmetry). The peak at 50 ppm is in the C–N range (CH bonded to N), the 23 ppm peak is a C–C carbon (the two equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ of an isopropyl group), and the 35 ppm peak is the N–$\text{CH}_3$ carbon.

**$^1$H NMR:**
- 2.55 ppm, 3H singlet: a $\text{CH}_3$ with no neighbouring H, shifted into the 2.5–3.1 ppm range, so it is bonded to N: N–$\text{CH}_3$.
- 2.9 ppm, 1H multiplet: a CH bonded to N with many neighbouring H (six from two $\text{CH}_3$ groups → septet).
- 1.15 ppm, 6H doublet: two equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ groups split by one neighbouring H. Together with the 1H multiplet this is an isopropyl group, $-\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$, bonded to N.
- 3.25 ppm, 1H singlet: the N–H proton (no splitting; within the 1–5 ppm range for R–NHR).

Putting the fragments together: $\text{CH}_3\text{-NH-CH(CH}_3)_2$, $N$-methylpropan-2-amine.
